questions.question: Orbit calculations use the gravitational parameter μ = GM of the central body in place of G and M separately. Why?
options: The product GM is measured precisely from the motion of moons and spacecraft
μ also contains the mass of the spacecraft, which G and M leave out
G has a different value for each planet, so it is combined with that planet's mass
μ has no units, so using it removes unit errors from orbit calculations
questions.explanation: Orbits reveal the product GM, not G or M alone. The spacecraft mass is left out of the two-body model, G is the same everywhere, and μ carries units of km3/s2.

questions.question: A satellite at 300 km altitude loses a little altitude on every revolution. Which assumption of the two-body problem does this effect break?
options: Gravity is the only force acting on the satellite
Each body is a point mass or an evenly layered sphere
Only two bodies are present
The satellite is so light that Earth does not move in response to it
questions.explanation: Air drag is a force other than gravity, and it takes energy from the orbit. Earth's bulge (not a point mass) turns the orbit plane, and the Moon and the Sun (more bodies) matter most for high orbits; neither lowers a low orbit steadily.

questions.question: A satellite orbits Earth (R = 6,378 km) with a perigee altitude of 350 km and an apogee altitude of 2,700 km. What is the semi-major axis of its orbit?
questions.explanation: Radii from the center: rp = 6,728 km and ra = 9,078 km, so a = (rp + ra)/2 = 7,903 km. 1,525 km averages the altitudes, 15,806 km forgets to halve the sum, and 1,175 km is half the difference, the distance c from the center to the focus.

questions.section: Where the orbit sits in space
questions.question: Which orbital element gives the tilt of the orbit plane from the equator of an Earth orbit?
options: The inclination i
The argument of periapsis ω
The right ascension of the ascending node Ω
The true anomaly θ
questions.explanation: The inclination is the angle between the two planes, measured at the ascending node. Ω locates the node in the equatorial plane, ω turns the ellipse within its own plane, and θ locates the spacecraft on the orbit.

questions.question: Two satellites orbit the same planet. The semi-major axis of satellite A is four times that of satellite B. How many times longer is the period of A?
questions.explanation: T grows as a3/2, and 43/2 = 8. The answer 4 treats the period as proportional to a, 16 as proportional to a2, and 2 as proportional to the square root of a.

questions.question: Two Earth satellites have the same semi-major axis. One orbit is a circle; the other is an ellipse with e = 0.5. How do their specific orbital energies compare?
options: They are equal, because the energy depends only on a
The ellipse has more energy, because it reaches farther from Earth
The circle has more energy, because its speed never drops
They cannot be compared without the masses of the satellites
questions.explanation: The energy depends only on the semi-major axis. The ellipse trades speed for altitude around its orbit, but the sum stays the same and equals that of the circle. Specific orbital energy is per unit mass, so no mass is needed.

questions.question: A satellite moves on a circular orbit 1,000 km above Earth (μ = 3.986 × 105 km3/s2, R = 6,378 km). What is its speed?
questions.explanation: With r = 7,378 km, vc = √(μ/r) = 7.350 km/s. 19.96 km/s uses the altitude as the radius, 10.39 km/s is the escape speed √(2μ/r), and 7.905 km/s is the circular speed at Earth's surface.

questions.question: At one point of its path, a spacecraft moves faster than the escape speed at that radius. What is its trajectory?
options: A hyperbola: e > 1, positive specific orbital energy, and it does not return
A long ellipse: e < 1, negative specific orbital energy, and it returns much later
A parabola: e = 1 and zero specific orbital energy
A circle, provided the velocity is perpendicular to the radius
questions.explanation: Above the escape speed, v2/2 is larger than μ/r, so the energy is positive and the path is a hyperbola. An ellipse needs a speed below the escape speed, a parabola exactly the escape speed, and a circle exactly the circular speed.
